title: Operation Christmas
medium: Lit trees in the jungle, then TV and radio
hook: Christmas lights in the jungle, asking fighters to come home.
before: FARC was the oldest guerrilla group in the world. Interviews with former members showed that Christmas was when fighters felt most homesick.
idea: In December 2010 Lowe SSP3 and the ministry wrapped nine tall trees near jungle paths in lights that switched on as people passed, with a banner: if Christmas can come to the jungle, you can come home. Demobilise.
shift: An army spoke to its enemy as people with families. Two more Christmas operations followed in 2011 and 2013.
measure: Demobilisations credited to the three operations in the IPA paper, with an estimated $8.6m return to the government
evidence: The IPA paper credits the operations with 711 demobilisations and estimates the return to the state. A later academic study of almost 20,000 deserters from 2002 to 2017 found no measurable effect of the Christmas campaigns on demobilisation rates. Both are on the record.
lesson: Find the moment your audience is most open, and speak to the person, not the role.
test: The IPA paper estimated demobilisations and the financial return. An independent study later tested the effect against long-run desertion data.
links: Read the history and the later study · Wikipedia
Explore Lowe SSP3’s original case film · D&AD
memorable: Lights coming on in the dark as someone walks past. It is a Christmas card that finds you.
metric_label: Fighters who demobilised across three Christmas operations
take: The most important case in the archive, and the most honest lesson in evidence. An award-winning model and an academic study disagree, and both deserve to be read.
credit: IPA 2011 · Gold, and IPA 2014 · Silver · Lowe SSP3 and MullenLowe London for the Colombian Ministry of Defence
data_source: A government talking to guerrillas at Christmas

image.alt: A red banner hanging in the jungle asks people to come home for Christmas
image.credit: Lowe SSP3 and the Colombian Ministry of Defence, Operation Christmas (2010) · D&AD case-film still

title: Havaianas Top
hook: Brazil’s cheapest sandal became something people paid double for.
before: Havaianas were rubber flip-flops seen as footwear for people who couldn’t afford shoes. Sales had been falling since the late 1980s.
idea: In 1994 Alpargatas launched Havaianas Top, a range in bright single colours at twice the basic price, with advertising featuring young, glamorous Brazilians.
shift: The same rubber sandal became a badge of Brazilian style, and later a global fashion brand.
measure: Annual unit sales, as reported in the company history
evidence: Unit sales rose sharply after the relaunch, and international growth followed from 2000. Sources differ on the exact figures, and the product, price and advertising all changed together.
lesson: Sometimes the product doesn’t need changing. The story around it does.
test: The record is reported unit sales before and after the relaunch.
memorable: A flip-flop on a fashion shoot, in colours that looked like Brazil.

creative.label: Watch the 1994 Havaianas advert with Malu Mader and Luiz Fernando Guimarães
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Pairs sold in 1999, up from 70m in 1993
take: Lucozade in Edition 06 did this with a drink. Havaianas did it with the cheapest thing a Brazilian could wear.
data_source: A poor man’s sandal, relaunched as fashion

image.alt: Blue Havaianas sandal on sand, framed by seashells and curved marks
image.credit: Havaianas print advertising · Eugênio Mohallem’s portfolio

title: Will It Blend?
hook: A blender company that blended an iPhone.
before: Blendtec made powerful blenders for kitchens and businesses, with almost no consumer marketing budget.
idea: Founder Tom Dickson, in a lab coat, blended marbles, rakes and later an iPhone, asking each time: will it blend?
shift: A product test became entertainment, and a small manufacturer became famous online.
measure: The company’s reported rise in retail sales within about two years. Self-reported, with an inconsistent timeframe
evidence: The sales figure comes from the company and is repeated in trade write-ups with different timeframes. Treat it as self-reported.
lesson: If your product does something extraordinary, film it doing that.
test: There is no independent record, only the company’s reported sales.
memorable: The smoke when the iPhone goes in, and the founder’s calm voice.

creative.label: Watch ‘Will It Blend? iPhone’ on Blendtec’s channel

metric_label: Rise in retail sales, as reported by the company
take: Sony’s balls in Edition 01 cost a fortune. This cost about $50 and did the same job: show the product being brilliant.

image.alt: An iPhone in the jar of a Blendtec blender
image.credit: Blendtec, Will It Blend? iPhone (2007) · original film still

title: M-Pesa
hook: A text message that became a bank.
before: Many Kenyans could use a mobile phone but had no bank account. Sending money home meant carrying cash or trusting a bus driver.
idea: In March 2007 Safaricom launched M-Pesa, developed with Vodafone, so people could store and send money by text, cashing in and out at local agents.
shift: A phone network became the way a country handles money.
measure: 194,000 households, as estimated in a 2016 study in Science
evidence: Economists used the uneven spread of M-Pesa agents as a natural experiment and estimated that access lifted 194,000 households out of poverty, with the biggest gains for households headed by women. It measures the product’s effect on lives, not the marketing.
lesson: The most powerful brand idea can be a service people couldn’t live without.
test: Researchers compared households with and without nearby agents between 2008 and 2010.
links: Read how Vodafone and Safaricom developed M-Pesa · Vodafone
memorable: Green agent kiosks on every corner, doing what banks never did.

creative.label: Watch ‘Why M-PESA Succeeded’ on Safaricom’s channel

impact_source: Read about the study · Innovations for Poverty Action
metric_label: Of Kenyan households lifted out of poverty
take: Product first would have claimed this one. I put it here because the turning point is the place: a service built for how Kenyans actually live.

image.alt: A customer holds an early mobile phone as a cash note changes hands
image.credit: Early M-Pesa transaction photograph (2008) · Vodafone archive

title: Singles’ Day
hook: A brand turned a joke about being single into the world’s biggest shopping day.
before: 11 November was an informal ‘singles’ day’ among Chinese students. Alibaba’s Taobao Mall wanted a reason to shop between the autumn holidays and the new year.
idea: In 2009 Daniel Zhang’s team ran a one-day sale on 11.11 with 27 merchants.
shift: Alibaba didn’t just join a moment, it created one, and owned it.
measure: Sales in 2009, as widely reported. By 2020 the festival reported 498bn yuan
evidence: The growth is reported in Alibaba’s own figures and the press. It shows the festival’s scale, not what any single campaign added.
lesson: If no moment fits your brand, make one people want to keep.
test: The record is Alibaba’s announced sales each year.
links: Read how it grew · The Business of Fashion
memorable: A date that looks like four people standing alone.

creative.label: Watch Alibaba Group explain how the 11.11 shopping festival grew
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the history · Free Malaysia Today
metric_label: Sales on the first Singles’ Day
take: Edition 02 had KitKat owning the tea break. This is the same move at a scale nobody could have imagined in 1958.
data_source: A shopping day a brand invented

title: Kitto Katsu
hook: In Japan, KitKat sounds like ‘you will surely win’.
before: Japanese students noticed that KitKat sounds like ‘kitto katsu’, roughly ‘you will surely win’, and began giving the bars as good-luck charms before exams. Sales rose every January.
idea: Nestlé Japan leaned in. In 2009, with Japan Post and J. Walter Thompson Japan, it launched Kit Mail: KitKats that could be posted from around 20,000 post offices, with space for a message.
shift: A chocolate bar became a token of encouragement, sent through the post.
measure: Roughly the number of post offices in the scheme. A fact, not a result
evidence: The exam-season sales rise is widely reported, and an earlier ‘lucky charm’ promotion won an Asian marketing effectiveness award in 2005. No public figure isolates the effect of Kit Mail.
lesson: Listen to what people already do with your product, then make it easier.
test: There is no published effectiveness record for Kit Mail, only awards and reports of the sales pattern.
links: Read about Kit Kat postage · Japan Today
Watch the later Kit Mail Hologram campaign · MAD STARS
memorable: A chocolate bar with a handwritten note, arriving the week of an exam.

creative.label: Watch the 2009 Kit Kat Mail case film from Nestlé Japan and JWT Tokyo
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: The brand didn’t invent this. Students did. The smart part was Nestlé noticing, and having the humility to follow.
credit: Nestlé Japan and Japan Post · J. Walter Thompson Japan
data_source: A chocolate bar given a job by a culture

image.alt: Pink Kit Kat Mail packages displayed at a Japanese post office counter
image.credit: Nestlé Japan and JWT Tokyo, Kit Kat Mail (2009) · case-film still

title: Our Blades Are F***ing Great
hook: A cheap video that made razors funny, and made a start-up worth a billion.
before: Razor blades were expensive, locked in cabinets and sold by giants such as Gillette.
idea: Founder Michael Dubin starred in a deadpan launch video for a razor subscription, walking through a warehouse explaining why paying more is pointless.
shift: A start-up with no ad budget made the category leader look overpriced.
measure: Orders after the video launched, as widely reported. Unilever bought the company in 2016 for a reported $1bn
evidence: The orders and the sale are widely reported. They show the video started a business. They don’t separate the video from the subscription model and the price.
lesson: If you can’t outspend the leader, out-talk them.
test: The record is early orders and the later acquisition.
memorable: A founder who talks to the camera like a friend who has had enough.

creative.label: Watch ‘Our Blades Are F***ing Great’ on Dollar Shave Club’s channel

impact_source: Read the acquisition report · NBC News
take: Ninety seconds that every challenger brand has tried to copy since. Few did it with this much confidence.

image.alt: Michael Dubin stands beside warehouse equipment in the Dollar Shave Club launch film
image.credit: Dollar Shave Club, Our Blades Are F***ing Great (2012) · original film still

title: The Ice Bucket Challenge
hook: A bucket of ice water that raised over $100m for a rare disease.
before: ALS, motor neurone disease, was little known and underfunded.
idea: In summer 2014 people filmed themselves pouring ice water over their heads, named friends to do the same and asked for donations. People living with ALS and their friends helped it spread.
shift: A charity’s cause became a summer ritual for millions.
measure: Funds raised during the challenge, of which about $77m went to research
evidence: The money raised is well recorded, and part of it funded research that identified a gene linked to ALS. The ALS Association itself called that discovery significant but not a breakthrough.
lesson: Give people a part to play that is easy, visible and fun to pass on.
test: The record is donations during and after the challenge.
links: Watch the ALS Association explain how the challenge began
memorable: The gasp. Everyone knows the sound of ice water hitting someone’s head.

creative.label: Watch the 10th anniversary film on the ALS Association’s channel

impact_source: Read about the funding and the discovery · TIME
metric_label: Raised for the ALS Association in 2014
take: Nobody at the charity designed this, and that’s the point. The best participation ideas belong to the people doing them.

image.alt: Pete Frates, a co-founder of the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge
image.credit: Pete Frates · The ALS Association’s history of the Ice Bucket Challenge

title: Like Milk, but Made for Humans
hook: A small oat drink brand got sued, and published the lawsuit.
before: Oatly was a small Swedish company selling oat drinks to a niche of health and lactose-free shoppers.
idea: Under chief executive Toni Petersson, Oatly wrote packaging and ads that talked like a person and teased the dairy industry. Sweden’s dairy lobby sued over lines such as ‘like milk, but made for humans’.
shift: Oatly lost the case and turned it into publicity, publishing the lawsuit. The attack made the small brand look brave.
measure: The year the lawsuit was filed. A fact, not a result
evidence: Bloomberg reported that Oatly’s sales grew significantly after the lawsuit was filed. No public figure isolates the effect, and the line was later restricted by regulators in some markets.
lesson: A small brand’s strongest asset can be a big enemy.
test: The record is press reports of sales after the lawsuit.
links: Read about the UK campaign · The Drum
memorable: Packaging that reads like a letter from a slightly cheeky friend.

creative.label: Watch Toni Petersson sing Wow No Cow on Oatly’s channel
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: The year Sweden’s dairy lobby sued
take: Edition 05 is full of brands that picked a fight and lost. Oatly lost the court case and won the argument.
data_source: A small Swedish brand sued by the dairy lobby

title: Project 84
hook: 84 figures on a rooftop, for the 84 men lost to suicide every week.
before: Suicide was the biggest killer of men under 45 in the UK, and the silence around it was making it worse.
idea: The Campaign Against Living Miserably and adam&eveDDB placed 84 life-size figures by the artist Mark Jenkins on the rooftops of ITV’s South Bank studios in March 2018, with This Morning as a partner.
shift: An image, not an ad, broke the silence. The UK appointed its first minister for suicide prevention later that year.
measure: The societal payback estimated in the IPA paper, which also credits the campaign with preventing 283 suicides
evidence: The IPA paper estimates 283 suicides prevented and a social payback of £5,119 for every £1, on a total budget of £100,000. Estimates of this kind rest on modelling assumptions, and the paper sets them out.
lesson: A single image, placed where people can’t ignore it, can do what a campaign budget can’t.
test: The IPA paper modelled the social value of suicides prevented against the cost of the work.
memorable: Figures standing at the edge of a roof, seen from the street. You look up, and then you understand.

creative.label: Watch ‘The Unveiling of Project 84’ on This Morning’s channel
creative.heading: Film

take: The strongest proof in this edition came from the smallest budget. When it matters this much, someone makes sure it is measured.

image.alt: Figures on the roof of ITV’s South Bank studios for Project 84
